snippet.title: Investing for Beginners (It is Easy!)
snippet.description:
Slide 1 (0:00): Investing is NOT COMPLICATED!!! Watch this and you will know the importance of investing, how to invest, and how exactly investing grows your money.
Slide 2 (0:30): Bad news for your money...Inflation, which is almost a guarantee in our economy, decreases the value of your money. Bank accounts, even high yield interest savings account, cannot keep up with inflation.
Slide 3 (0:48): The average annual inflation rate is 3.22%. At this rate, prices double every 20 years. Many years in our country's past have been far worse than this average, including the 13.5% inflation in 1980. 
Slide 4 (1:18): Great news for your money! The S&P 500, which is a collection of about 500 major companies in the US, has averaged 9.8% returns year over year. If you invest in this, your money will grow 6.6% each year on average EVEN AFTER ACCOUNTING FOR inflation.
Slide 5 (1:49): There are three simple ways to invest. Stocks, ETFs, or Index/Mutual Funds (Index Funds are better in my opinion).
Slide 6 (2:01): Buying a stock is buying ownership in a company. If that company becomes more valuable, then you can sell your piece of the company for more than you paid for it.  
Slide 7 (2:40): ETFs are a bunch of stocks put into one. They trade just like a stock but are much more diverse. If one company's value crashes, your ETF wont crash because there are other companies in the ETF bringing the fund's value higher. 
Slide 8 (3:30): Funds (index or mutual) are very similar to ETFs. For example, you can invest in the S&P 500 either in an ETF or a fund. But, funds will require a minimum investment (typically $3,000 for Vanguard funds). Once that minimum is invested, the minimum for additional investment is $1, which is unlike ETFs or stocks because you have to buy a full share of them to invest. This makes auto investing / investing on a budget much easier.
Slide 9 (5:26): Your money grows through capital gains which is simply the price of the investment when you sell minus the price you paid when you bought it. 
Slide 10 (6:10): Dividends are the second way your money grows. Some companies will pay part of their profits back to investors. 


Disclaimer: Investments do not always increase your money's value. There will be periods where they lose value. However, at any given time, the market is more likely to go up than go down (based off historical data). Be patient! snippet.title: Share Buyback Rules Changed in 2026! Tax, ₹2 Lakh Retail Limit & Hidden Benefits Explained
snippet.description:
Share buybacks can offer retail investors an opportunity to tender their shares at a fixed price, sometimes at a premium to the prevailing market price. But do you understand the new tax rules, retail shareholder reservation and the risks involved?

In this video, we explain share buybacks in India, with a special focus on **tender-offer buybacks** and the important changes effective 1 April 2026.

We also look at three recent tender-offer buybacks with upcoming record dates (as of 13 November 2026):

**1. Global Education**
- Buyback price: ₹162 per share
- Buyback size: Approximately ₹23.90 crore
- Record date: 18 November 2026

**2. Medi Assist Healthcare Services**
- Buyback price: ₹425 per share
- Buyback size: Approximately ₹49.27 crore
- Record date: 20 November 2026

**3. Zee Entertainment Enterprises (ZEEL)**
- Buyback price: ₹91 per share
- Buyback size: Up to ₹600 crore
- Record date: 25 November 2026

These are examples of announced offers, not buy recommendations. A buyback price premium does not guarantee a profit. Market price movements, acceptance ratio, taxes and transaction costs all matter.

**What you will learn in this video:**
- Open-market vs tender-offer buybacks
- How buyback taxation changed from 1 April 2026
- Tax treatment of accepted and unaccepted shares
- How the ₹2 lakh retail shareholder limit is calculated
- Why the retail category can have a separate reservation
- How your PAN determines retail eligibility across brokers
- Risks of buying shares just before a record date

**Important:** Always verify the latest company announcements, record dates, offer documents and market prices before making an investment decision. Buyback details and timelines may change.

snippet.title: COVID-19 Weekly Update #16 (The Personal Finance Show)
snippet.description:
Week 16 of the COVID-19 series features my friends Brynn Byrne and Aaron Yeger, co-hosts of the new podcast "That Was a Show?".

We talk about Brynn and Aaron's COVID-19 experience and how the pandemic has affected their personal finances, but mostly I wanted them on to talk about their awesome new podcast.  I can't explain it better than them so here's the summary direct from their podcast page:

The podcast about failed or forgotten sitcoms from the 80s and 90s. Many sitcoms have stood the test of time and have millions of adoring fans—but those shows were diamonds in the rough. This podcast is not about those diamonds, it's about the rough. Some sitcoms were briefly popular in their time, some were cancelled almost immediately. You probably won't recognize most of these, and you'll say 'that was a show?'

As I said in the episode, it's important that podcasts promote other podcast, especially those of a different genre.  I listen to a lot of personal finance shows but I also listen to shows like This American Life, Invisibilia, "How Did That Get Made?", and other non-financial podcasts.  These podcasts are doing fine on their own but there are some podcasts that are excellent but people just don't know about them yet.  If you are a child of the 80s and 90s and enjoy talking about television, you will love this show like I do.

snippet.title: The $100k Threshold: Why Saving First Beats Investing
snippet.description:
Why 8% compound interest in an S&P 500 index fund, Roth IRA, or 401(k) feels completely flat under $10,000, and the math to reach $100,000.

If you have $4,700 saved and earn an 8% annual return, your money makes $376 a year. That comes out to $1.03 a day. One $32 dinner order on a delivery app wipes out a full month of market gains. It is the main reason so many people in their twenties give up on index funds and throw rent money at prediction markets or meme coins instead.

Compound interest is not broken, but it does have a mechanical minimum. Until your portfolio crosses the point where annual investment returns rival your monthly paycheck deposits, raw savings rate does almost all the heavy lifting.

In this episode, we put two 25-year-olds earning the exact same $58,000 starting salary ($3,850 a month net after FICA and taxes) into The Blueprint Simulator for ten years. We test manual willpower saving against an automated 3-step paycheck system using 2026 IRS contribution limits ($7,500 Roth IRA, $24,500 401(k), and a 4.00% APY high-yield savings account buffer).

snippet.title: How One or Two Extra EMIs Can Save Lakhs on Your Home Loan
snippet.description:
Did you know that paying just one or two extra EMIs on your home loan each year can save you lakhs of rupees in interest and help you become debt-free years earlier?
Home loans are amortized, meaning in the early years, most of your EMI goes towards interest rather than reducing the principal. By prepaying even a small extra amount—like one full EMI annually—you directly reduce the outstanding principal. This lowers the interest calculated on the remaining balance, creating a powerful compounding effect in your favor.
For example, consider a ₹50 lakh home loan at 8.5% interest for 20 years. Your regular EMI would be around ₹43,000, and total interest paid over the tenure could exceed ₹46 lakh.
But if you pay just one extra EMI (about ₹43,000) every year, you could:

Reduce your loan tenure by 3-4 years
Save over ₹8-10 lakh in interest

And if you manage two extra EMIs annually, the savings can climb to ₹15 lakh or more, shortening the tenure even further!
The key is to start early—prepayments in the initial years yield the maximum benefits since that's when the interest burden is highest. Most banks allow partial prepayments on floating-rate home loans without penalties, so check with your lender.
Small consistent efforts like this can turn your long-term loan into a shorter, cheaper journey to owning your home outright. Start planning your prepayments today and watch those savings add up!
